1.solution:
\(50\) mL of a \(16.9\%\) (w/v) solution holds \(8.45\) g of \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\), that is \(\dfrac{8.45}{169} = 0.05\) mol.

\(50\) mL of a \(7.45\%\) solution holds \(3.725\) g of KCl, that is \(\dfrac{3.725}{74.5} = 0.05\) mol.

\(\mathrm{AgNO_3 + KCl \rightarrow AgCl\downarrow + KNO_3}\) reacts \(1:1\), so \(0.05\) mol of AgCl precipitates: \(0.05 \times 143.3 = 7.17\) g, about \(7\) g.

2.subtopic: Quantum Mechanical Model, de Broglie, Heisenberg and Quantum Numbers

3.solution: Atomic radius falls across a period as the nuclear charge grows, so the halogens (group 17) are the smallest in each period. Noble gases (group 18) are quoted as van der Waals radii, which are larger than covalent radii, so they do not count as the smallest.

4.solution: Across a period electrons enter the same shell while the nuclear charge rises by one each step. The outer electrons are pulled in more strongly, so atomic size decreases from left to right.

5.subtopic: Dipole Moment, Polarity and Intermolecular Forces
5.solution:
\(\mathrm{BF_3}\) is trigonal planar and symmetric, so its dipole moment is zero.

In \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) the N-H bond dipoles point towards N, the same way as the lone-pair moment, so they add (about \(1.47\) D). In \(\mathrm{NF_3}\) the N-F bond dipoles point away from N, against the lone-pair moment, so they partly cancel (about \(0.23\) D).

Order: \(\mathrm{NH_3 > NF_3 > BF_3}\).

6.subtopic: Real Gases, Dalton's Law and KTG

7.subtopic: Enthalpy and Relation Between ΔH and ΔU
7.solution:
Only gases count in \(\Delta n_g\): \(\Delta n_g = 2 - 3 = -1\).

\(\Delta U = \Delta H - \Delta n_g RT = -1366.5 - (-1)(8.314 \times 10^{-3})(300) = -1366.5 + 2.49 = -1364.0\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\).

8.solution:
When a gas is adsorbed its molecules lose their freedom of movement and are held on the surface, so the disorder falls and \(\Delta S < 0\).

Dissolving sugar, decomposing 2 mol of gas into 4 mol of gas, and turning a solid into a gas all increase disorder.

9.solution: Free energy, enthalpy and entropy are state functions: they depend on the amount of matter but not on the path. Heat is a path function, and the heat exchanged also grows with the amount of matter, so heat is the answer.

10.subtopic: Ionic Equilibrium, Ka, Kb and Degree of Dissociation
10.solution:
\(c = \dfrac{0.2}{2} = 0.1\ \mathrm{M}\).

For a weak acid \(\alpha = \sqrt{\dfrac{K_a}{c}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1.5 \times 10^{-5}}{0.1}} = \sqrt{1.5 \times 10^{-4}} = 0.01225\), so the dissociation is \(1.22\%\).

12.solution: The weaker the acid, the stronger its conjugate base. HCl, \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\) and \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) are strong acids, so \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\), \(\mathrm{NO_3^-}\) and \(\mathrm{HSO_4^-}\) are very weak bases. Acetic acid is a weak acid, so \(\mathrm{CH_3COO^-}\) is the strongest base of the four.

13.subtopic: Group 1 Alkali Metals, Properties and Reactivity
13.solution: Atomic size increases down a group as a new shell is added each period. Of Na, K, Rb and Cs, sodium is highest in group 1, so it is the smallest.

14.subtopic: Reactions of Alkenes, Addition, Oxidation and Ozonolysis
14.solution: Acidified permanganate cleaves the C=C bond and oxidises each fragment fully. But-2-ene, \(\mathrm{CH_3CH{=}CHCH_3}\), splits into two \(\mathrm{CH_3CHO}\) units, each oxidised to \(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}\). The product is acetic acid.

15.subtopic: Reactions of Alkenes, Addition, Oxidation and Ozonolysis
15.solution: Markownikoff's rule decides where H and Br go only when the alkene is unsymmetrical. But-2-ene, hex-3-ene and ethene are symmetrical, so both ways of adding give the same product. 2-Methylpropene, \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2C{=}CH_2}\), is unsymmetrical: H adds to the \(\mathrm{CH_2}\) and Br to the carbon with two methyl groups, giving 2-bromo-2-methylpropane.

16.subtopic: Preparation of Alkanes, Wurtz, Grignard and Decarboxylation
16.solution: In a Wurtz reaction with \(\mathrm{RX}\) and \(\mathrm{R'X}\), the alkyl groups can couple in three ways: \(\mathrm{R{-}R}\), \(\mathrm{R'{-}R'}\) and \(\mathrm{R{-}R'}\). So three alkanes can form.

17.subtopic: Side-Chain Reactions, Oxidation and Other Transformations
17.solution: Heating n-hexane over \(\mathrm{V_2O_5}\) (or \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_3}\)) on alumina at about \(773\) K closes the chain into a ring and removes hydrogen (aromatisation): \(\mathrm{C_6H_{14} \rightarrow C_6H_6 + 4H_2}\). The product is benzene.

18.solution:
For fcc, \(Z = 4\), and \(\rho = \dfrac{ZM}{a^3 N_A}\), so \(M = \dfrac{\rho a^3 N_A}{Z}\).

\(a^3 = (3.608 \times 10^{-8})^3 = 4.697 \times 10^{-23}\ \mathrm{cm^3}\).

\(M = \dfrac{8.92 \times 4.697 \times 10^{-23} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}}{4} = \dfrac{252.3}{4} = 63.1\) g/mol, about \(63\) g/mol (copper).

19.solution:
Density times volume of a unit cell is the mass of one unit cell, \(2.5 \times 10^{-22}\) g.

Number of unit cells in \(1\) g \(= \dfrac{1}{2.5 \times 10^{-22}} = 4.0 \times 10^{21}\).

20.subtopic: Crystal Defects, Magnetic Properties and Semiconductors
20.solution: In a Schottky defect equal numbers of cations and anions are missing from their sites. The crystal stays stoichiometric and electrically neutral, and the defect is a vacancy defect. Because ions leave the crystal while its volume stays the same, the density decreases. So "density remains unchanged" is not a characteristic.

21.subtopic: Van't Hoff Factor and Abnormal Molar Mass
21.solution:
\(\mathrm{K_4[Fe(CN)_6] \rightarrow 4K^+ + [Fe(CN)_6]^{4-}}\), so one formula unit gives \(n = 5\) ions.

\(i = 1 + (n - 1)\alpha = 1 + 4 \times 0.6 = 3.4\).

22.solution:
Both solutes are non-electrolytes in the same solvent, so equal boiling points need equal molalities.

Urea: \(m = \dfrac{5/60}{0.100} = 0.833\) mol/kg.

Glucose: \(\dfrac{w/180}{0.120} = 0.833\), so \(w = 0.833 \times 0.120 \times 180 = 18\) g.

23.subtopic: Van't Hoff Factor and Abnormal Molar Mass
23.solution:
The ratio of theoretical to observed molar mass is the van't Hoff factor \(i\). For complete dissociation \(i\) equals the number of ions per formula unit.

KCl and \(\mathrm{MgSO_4}\) give 2 ions, \(\mathrm{K_2SO_4 \rightarrow 2K^+ + SO_4^{2-}}\) gives 3, and \(\mathrm{Al_2(SO_4)_3}\) gives 5. So the answer is \(\mathrm{K_2SO_4}\).

24.subtopic: Molar Conductivity, Kohlrausch's Law and Degree of Dissociation

25.subtopic: Batteries, Primary, Secondary and Fuel Cells
25.solution: The mercury cell is a primary dry cell with a zinc-mercury amalgam anode and a cathode of HgO mixed with carbon, where HgO is reduced to Hg. Its electrolyte is a paste of KOH and ZnO, which is strongly alkaline, not acidic. So statement (C) is not true.

27.subtopic: First-Order Kinetics, Rate Constant and Half-Life
27.solution:
For a first order reaction \(t = \dfrac{2.303}{k}\log\dfrac{[A]_0}{[A]}\).

\(90\%\) completion: \(\log 10 = 1\). \(99.9\%\) completion: \(\log 1000 = 3\). So the second time is three times the first: \(3\) hours.

28.subtopic: Rate Law, Order, Molecularity and Rate Expression

29.solution: For a zero order reaction \([A]_t = [A]_0 - kt\). This is a straight line of \([A]_t\) against \(t\) with slope \(-k\).

30.solution: Nanostructures are classed by how many dimensions lie outside the nanoscale. A nanotube is nanoscale in two dimensions and long in one, so it is a one-dimensional nanostructure, like nanowires and nanorods.

31.subtopic: Colloids, Classification, Coagulation and Hardy-Schulze Rule
31.solution:
Brownian motion is the random zig-zag movement of colloidal particles: (A) - (III).

The Tyndall effect is the scattering of light by colloidal particles: (B) - (IV).

Electrophoresis is the movement of colloidal particles in an electric field: (C) - (II).

Dialysis removes dissolved impurities from a sol through a semipermeable membrane: (D) - (I).

32.subtopic: Inner Transition Elements, Lanthanoids and Actinoids
32.solution: In the actinoids the 5f, 6d and 7s levels are close in energy, so a varying number of electrons from all three can be lost or shared. This gives actinoids a wider range of oxidation states than lanthanoids, whose 4f electrons are buried deeper.

33.subtopic: Inner Transition Elements, Lanthanoids and Actinoids
33.solution: Across the lanthanides each added electron enters the 4f subshell while the nuclear charge rises by one. The diffuse 4f orbitals shield one another poorly, so the effective nuclear charge on the outer electrons rises and the size shrinks steadily. The cause is the poor shielding of one 4f electron by another.

34.subtopic: Colour, Magnetic Properties and Spin-Only Formula
34.solution:
\(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) is \(3d^9\), with one unpaired electron.

\(\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} = \sqrt{1 \times 3} = 1.73\) BM.

35.subtopic: Oxidation State, Coordination Number and IUPAC Nomenclature
35.solution:
Ethylenediamine and oxalate are both bidentate, so the coordination number is \(2 \times 2 + 2 = 6\).

The complex ion carries \(+1\) (one \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\) outside). With en neutral and oxalate \(-2\): \(x + 0 - 2 = +1\), so \(x = +3\).

Sum \(= 6 + 3 = 9\).

36.subtopic: Bonding Theories, EAN, Crystal Field, Hybridization and Magnetism
36.solution: In \(\mathrm{K_4[Fe(CN)_6]}\) each cyanide ligand donates a lone pair to \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\). The central ion accepts electron pairs, so it acts as a Lewis acid (the ligands are Lewis bases).

37.subtopic: Polyhalogen Compounds — Freon, DDT, War Gases
37.solution: Chloroform is slowly oxidised by air in light to phosgene: \(\mathrm{2CHCl_3 + O_2 \rightarrow 2COCl_2 + 2HCl}\). That is why it is stored in dark, full bottles.

38.solution: An alkyl halide is an alkane \(\mathrm{C}_n\mathrm{H}_{2n+2}\) with one H replaced by a halogen X, so its formula is \(\mathrm{C}_n\mathrm{H}_{2n+1}\mathrm{X}\).

39.solution:
This is the Reimer-Tiemann reaction run with carbon tetrachloride instead of chloroform. Phenol in aqueous NaOH reacts with \(\mathrm{CCl_4}\) at the ortho position to give a \(\mathrm{-CCl_3}\) group (A), which alkali hydrolyses to the carboxylate, giving sodium salicylate (B). Acidification gives salicylic acid, o-hydroxybenzoic acid (C), structure B.

(With chloroform the same reaction gives salicylaldehyde, structure A.)

40.solution: A dihydric alcohol has two OH groups. Ethylene glycol, \(\mathrm{HOCH_2CH_2OH}\), has two. Glycerol has three, sorbitol six and methanol one.

41.solution: The OH group activates the ring so strongly that bromine water substitutes all three ortho and para positions at once, giving a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol.

42.solution: In the Cannizzaro reaction an aldehyde with no \(\alpha\)-hydrogen (such as HCHO or \(\mathrm{C_6H_5CHO}\)), heated with concentrated alkali, disproportionates: one molecule is reduced to the alcohol and another oxidised to the salt of the carboxylic acid. So (A) is true.

43.solution: Alkyl groups are electron releasing. A ketone has two of them on the carbonyl carbon, which lowers its positive character (and crowds it), so it is less electrophilic than an aldehyde with one. Hence aldehydes react faster with nucleophiles.

44.solution:
KCN replaces iodide: \(\mathrm{CH_3I \rightarrow CH_3CN}\) (A, ethanenitrile).

Sodium in ethanol (Mendius reduction) reduces the nitrile to a primary amine: \(\mathrm{CH_3CN + 4[H] \rightarrow CH_3CH_2NH_2}\) (B, ethylamine).

45.subtopic: Chemical Reactions and Basicity of Amines
45.solution: Hinsberg's reagent is benzenesulphonyl chloride, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5SO_2Cl}\). It reacts differently with primary, secondary and tertiary amines, which lets the three be told apart.

46.subtopic: Nucleic Acids, DNA, RNA, Nucleotides and Bases
46.solution: The sugar-phosphate backbone is the same along every DNA strand. The information is coded in the order of the bases A, T, G and C along the strand, so it is carried by the sequence of nitrogenous bases.

47.solution: Hydroxylamine reacts with a carbonyl group to form an oxime. Glucose forms an oxime, which shows it has a carbonyl (C=O) group.

48.solution: Dacron (terylene) is a polyester made from ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid, so its units are joined by ester linkages. Orlon, Teflon and neoprene are addition polymers with a plain carbon chain.

49.solution: Vulcanization heats rubber with sulphur, which forms sulphur cross-links between the polymer chains. The cross-linked rubber is harder and stronger, with higher tensile strength and elasticity and less stickiness. Its plasticity falls rather than rises.

50.subtopic: Colloids, Classification, Coagulation and Hardy-Schulze Rule
50.solution: Cationic detergents are quaternary ammonium salts, such as cetyltrimethylammonium bromide. They are used in hair conditioners (and as germicides). Household and liquid detergents and toothpastes mostly use anionic detergents.

51.subtopic: Algebra of Complex Numbers — Conjugates, Powers of i and Cube Roots of Unity
51.solution:
Since \(\omega^3 = 1\), \(\dfrac{1}{\omega} = \omega^2\) and \(\dfrac{1}{\omega^2} = \omega\). The general term is \((r+1)(r+\omega^2)(r+\omega)\) for \(r = 1, 2, \ldots, n\).

\((r+\omega)(r+\omega^2) = r^2 + r(\omega+\omega^2) + \omega^3 = r^2 - r + 1\), using \(1 + \omega + \omega^2 = 0\).

So the term is \((r+1)(r^2 - r + 1) = r^3 + 1\), and the sum is \(\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}(r^3+1) = \left[\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}\right]^2 + n\).

52.subtopic: Counting Numbers and Geometric Figures — Digits, Divisibility, Points and Polygons
52.solution:
All five digits are used, so there are \(5! = 120\) such numbers.

A number is at most \(24000\) only if it starts with \(2\) and its second digit is less than \(4\), that is \(23\_\_\_\): \(3! = 6\) numbers. Every other number is greater than \(24000\).

Answer: \(120 - 6 = 114\).

53.subtopic: Solution of Triangle — Sine, Cosine and Projection Rules
53.solution:
With \(C = 90^\circ\): \(\sin A = \cos B = \dfrac{a}{c}\) and \(\cos A = \sin B = \dfrac{b}{c}\).

\(\sin(A - B) = \sin A\cos B - \cos A\sin B = \dfrac{a^2}{c^2} - \dfrac{b^2}{c^2} = \dfrac{a^2 - b^2}{c^2} = \dfrac{a^2 - b^2}{a^2 + b^2}\), since \(c^2 = a^2 + b^2\).

54.solution:
The expression is \(\tan(160^\circ - 110^\circ) = \tan 50^\circ = \cot 40^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\tan 40^\circ}\).

\(\tan 40^\circ = \dfrac{2\tan 20^\circ}{1 - \tan^2 20^\circ} = \dfrac{2P}{1 - P^2}\), so the value is \(\dfrac{1 - P^2}{2P}\).

55.solution:
\(\cos p\theta + \cos q\theta = 2\cos\dfrac{(p+q)\theta}{2}\cos\dfrac{(p-q)\theta}{2} = 0\).

So \(\dfrac{(p+q)\theta}{2} = (2n+1)\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) or \(\dfrac{(p-q)\theta}{2} = (2n+1)\dfrac{\pi}{2}\), giving \(\theta = \dfrac{(2n+1)\pi}{p \pm q}\).

56.subtopic: Forms of a Line, Intersections and Concurrency
56.solution:
Slope of BC \(= \dfrac{-2+3}{3-2} = 1\), so the altitude from A has slope \(-1\): \(y + 6 = -(x - 1)\), that is \(y = -x - 5\).

Slope of AC \(= \dfrac{-2+6}{3-1} = 2\), so the altitude from B has slope \(-\dfrac{1}{2}\): \(y + 3 = -\dfrac{1}{2}(x - 2)\), that is \(y = -\dfrac{x}{2} - 2\).

Solving: \(-x - 5 = -\dfrac{x}{2} - 2\) gives \(x = -6\), \(y = 1\). The orthocentre is \((-6, 1)\).

57.subtopic: Angle Between the Pair — Perpendicular Pairs, Lines at a Given Angle and the Bisectors
57.solution:
Here \(a = 1\), \(2h = -3\), \(b = 2\), so \(\tan\theta = \left|\dfrac{2\sqrt{h^2 - ab}}{a + b}\right| = \dfrac{2\sqrt{9/4 - 2}}{3} = \dfrac{2 \times \frac{1}{2}}{3} = \dfrac{1}{3}\).

Dividing numerator and denominator by \(\cos\theta\): \(\dfrac{3\tan\theta + 2}{3\tan\theta - 2} = \dfrac{1 + 2}{1 - 2} = -3\).

58.subtopic: Joint Equation of Two Lines — Product of Linear Factors and the Triangle They Form
58.solution:
\(2x^2 - 3xy - 2y^2 = (2x + y)(x - 2y)\), so the pair is \(y = -2x\) and \(y = \dfrac{x}{2}\). Their slopes multiply to \(-1\), so they meet at a right angle.

The third line \(3x - y = 7\) has slope \(3\). Its angle with \(y = \dfrac{x}{2}\): \(\tan\phi = \left|\dfrac{3 - \frac{1}{2}}{1 + \frac{3}{2}}\right| = 1\), so \(\phi = 45^\circ\).

A right angle and a \(45^\circ\) angle make the triangle right angled and isosceles.

59.subtopic: Equation of a Circle — Centre-Radius, General, Diameter and Parametric Forms
59.solution:
For a circle the coefficients of \(x^2\) and \(y^2\) are equal: \(a + 1 = 3\), so \(a = 2\).

The equation becomes \(3x^2 + 3y^2 - 6x + 9y + 6 = 0\), that is \(x^2 + y^2 - 2x + 3y + 2 = 0\).

Centre \(\left(1, -\dfrac{3}{2}\right)\); radius \(= \sqrt{1 + \dfrac{9}{4} - 2} = \sqrt{\dfrac{5}{4}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{2}\).

60.solution:
The tangent to \(x^2 - y^2 = 7\) at \((x_1, y_1)\) is \(xx_1 - yy_1 = 7\).

Comparing with \(4x + 3y = 7\): \(x_1 = 4\), \(y_1 = -3\) (and \(16 - 9 = 7\), so the point is on the hyperbola).

Sum of the coordinates \(= 4 - 3 = 1\).

61.solution:
Use \(\dfrac{4^x - 1}{x} \to \log 4\), \(\dfrac{\tan(x/4)}{x/4} \to 1\) and \(\dfrac{\log(1 + x^2/3)}{x^2/3} \to 1\):

\(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0}\dfrac{(4^x - 1)^3}{\tan\left(\frac{x}{4}\right)\log\left(1 + \frac{x^2}{3}\right)} = \dfrac{(\log 4)^3\,x^3}{\frac{x}{4} \cdot \frac{x^2}{3}} = 12(\log 4)^3 = 12 \times 8(\log 2)^3 = 96(\log 2)^3\).

So \(a = 2\), \(b = 3\) and \(a + b = 5\).

62.solution:
Inverse: \(\sim p \to \sim(q \to r)\). Its converse: \(\sim(q \to r) \to \sim p\), which is the contrapositive of the original, so it is equivalent to \(p \to (q \to r) \equiv \sim p \vee \sim q \vee r\).

A dual is taken of a statement written with \(\wedge\), \(\vee\) and \(\sim\) only, swapping \(\wedge\) and \(\vee\): the dual of \(\sim p \vee \sim q \vee r\) is \(\sim p \wedge \sim q \wedge r\).

\(\sim p \wedge \sim q \wedge r = \sim(p \vee q \vee \sim r) = \sim[p \vee (\sim r \vee q)] = \sim[p \vee (r \to q)]\).

63.solution:
With \(p = \mathrm{T}\), \(q = \mathrm{F}\), \(r = \mathrm{F}\): \(\sim(p \wedge \sim q) = \sim(\mathrm{T} \wedge \mathrm{T}) = \mathrm{F}\) and \(q \vee \sim r = \mathrm{F} \vee \mathrm{T} = \mathrm{T}\). So the statement is \(\mathrm{F} \vee \mathrm{T} = \mathrm{T}\).

Its dual swaps \(\wedge\) and \(\vee\): \(\sim(p \vee \sim q) \wedge (q \wedge \sim r)\). Here \(\sim(\mathrm{T} \vee \mathrm{T}) = \mathrm{F}\), so the dual is \(\mathrm{F}\).

Answer: True, False.

64.subtopic: Solution of Triangle — Half-Angle Formulas, Napier's Analogy and Area
64.solution:
\(\tan\dfrac{A}{2} = \sqrt{\dfrac{(s-b)(s-c)}{s(s-a)}}\) and \(\tan\dfrac{B}{2} = \sqrt{\dfrac{(s-a)(s-c)}{s(s-b)}}\), so \(\tan\dfrac{A}{2}\tan\dfrac{B}{2} = \dfrac{s-c}{s}\).

\(1 + \dfrac{s-c}{s} = \dfrac{2s - c}{s} = \dfrac{a + b}{s}\), so \(k = a + b\).

65.subtopic: Determinants, Cofactors and the Adjoint Identities
65.solution:
For a \(3 \times 3\) matrix, \(\det(\mathrm{adj}M) = (\det M)^2\).

A is upper triangular, so \(\det A = (2k-1)^3\) and \(\det(\mathrm{adj}A) = (2k-1)^6\).

B is skew-symmetric of odd order, so \(\det B = 0\) and \(\det(\mathrm{adj}B) = 0\).

So \((2k-1)^6 = 11^6\), giving \(2k - 1 = \pm 11\), \(k = 6\) or \(k = -5\). Then \(k - 5 = 1\) or \(-10\); only \(1\) is an option.

66.solution:
A is the rotation matrix \(R(\theta)\), and \(R(\alpha)R(\beta) = R(\alpha + \beta)\), so \(A^{-3} = R(-3\theta) = R\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\).

\(R\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \begin{bmatrix} \cos(-\pi/2) & -\sin(-\pi/2) \\ \sin(-\pi/2) & \cos(-\pi/2) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\).

67.subtopic: Inverse Trigonometric Identities — Sums, Substitution and Telescoping
67.solution:
\(5 - 2\sqrt{6} = (\sqrt{3} - \sqrt{2})^2\), so the argument is \(\dfrac{\sqrt{3} - \sqrt{2}}{1 + \sqrt{3}\sqrt{2}}\).

That is the form \(\dfrac{x - y}{1 + xy}\), so the left side is \(\tan^{-1}\sqrt{3} - \tan^{-1}\sqrt{2} = \dfrac{\pi}{3} - \tan^{-1}\sqrt{2}\). Hence \(k = \sqrt{2}\).

\(\sec^{-1}\sqrt{2} = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\).

68.subtopic: Composite Functions — f∘g, Iteration and Functional Identities
68.solution:
Put \(x = 0\): \(f(-y) + f(y) = 2f(0)f(y)\).

Put \(x = y = 0\): \(2f(0) = 2f(0)^2\), so \(f(0) = 1\) for any function that is not identically zero.

Then \(f(-y) + f(y) = 2f(y)\), that is \(f(-y) = f(y)\): f is even (for example \(f(x) = \cos x\)).

69.subtopic: Continuity at a Point — Finding f(c) and the Parameter
69.solution:
Put \(x = 1 - t\), \(t \to 0\): \(\cos(\pi x) = \cos(\pi - \pi t) = -\cos(\pi t)\).

\(f(1) = \displaystyle\lim_{t \to 0}\dfrac{1 - \cos(\pi t)}{\pi t^2} = \lim_{t \to 0}\dfrac{2\sin^2(\pi t/2)}{\pi t^2} = \dfrac{2}{\pi} \cdot \dfrac{\pi^2}{4} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\).

70.solution:
\(y = \log x^x = x\log x\), so \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \log x + 1\).

At \(x = e^2\): \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 2 + 1 = 3\), and its square is \(9\).

71.solution:
\(\sin x = \cos\left(x - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\), and for \(\dfrac{\pi}{2} < x < \pi\) the angle \(x - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) lies in \(\left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\), inside the principal range of \(\cos^{-1}\).

So \(y = x - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) and \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 1\).

74.subtopic: Rolle's Theorem and Mean Value Theorem

75.subtopic: Tangents, Normals, and the Slope of a Curve
75.solution:
The line \(2x - 2y = 3\) has slope \(1\), so the normal has slope \(1\) and the tangent slope \(-1\).

\(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \log x + 1 = -1\) gives \(\log x = -2\), \(x = e^{-2}\), and \(y = e^{-2} \times (-2) = -2e^{-2}\).

76.subtopic: Trigonometric Integrals - Rational and Substitution Forms
76.solution:
\(\sqrt{\sin 2x} = \sqrt{2}\sqrt{\tan x}\cos x\), so the integrand is \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\cdot\dfrac{\sec^4 x}{\sqrt{\tan x}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\cdot\dfrac{(1 + \tan^2 x)\sec^2 x}{\sqrt{\tan x}}\).

Put \(t = \tan x\), \(dt = \sec^2 x\,dx\): \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\displaystyle\int\left(t^{-1/2} + t^{3/2}\right)dt = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(2t^{1/2} + \dfrac{2}{5}t^{5/2}\right) + c = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{5}(t^2 + 5)\sqrt{t} + c\).

So \(p = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{5}\) and \(q = 5\).

77.solution:
\(1 + \sin x = \left(\sin\dfrac{x}{2} + \cos\dfrac{x}{2}\right)^2 = 2\sin^2\left(\dfrac{x}{2} + \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\).

So \(\sqrt{2}\sqrt{1 + \sin x} = 2\sin\left(\dfrac{x}{2} + \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\), and its integral is \(-4\cos\left(\dfrac{x}{2} + \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) + c\).

Hence \(a = \dfrac{1}{2}\), \(b = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\).

79.solution:
Let \(F = \displaystyle\int f(x)dx\) and \(G = \displaystyle\int g(x)dx\). By the product rule \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(FG) = fG + gF\).

Integrating both sides: \(FG = \displaystyle\int\left[f(x)\int g(x)dx + g(x)\int f(x)dx\right]dx\).

80.solution:
\(f(x) = \dfrac{d}{dx}e^x = e^x\) and \(g(x) = \dfrac{d}{dx}\cos x = -\sin x\).

The sum is \(\displaystyle\int e^x(\cos x - \sin x)\,dx\). Since \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(e^x\cos x) = e^x\cos x - e^x\sin x\), it equals \(e^x\cos x + c\).

81.subtopic: Evaluating Definite Integrals — Standard Forms, Algebraic Substitution and By Parts
81.solution:
Put \(e^x - 1 = t^2\): \(e^x\,dx = 2t\,dt\), and the limits become \(t = 0\) to \(t = 3\) (since \(e^{\log 10} - 1 = 9\)).

\(\displaystyle\int_0^3\dfrac{t \cdot 2t}{t^2 + 9}\,dt = 2\int_0^3\left(1 - \dfrac{9}{t^2 + 9}\right)dt = 2\left[t - 3\tan^{-1}\dfrac{t}{3}\right]_0^3 = 2\left(3 - \dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{3}{2}(4 - \pi)\).

82.subtopic: Odd and Even Integrands — Symmetric Limits
82.solution:
Replacing \(x\) by \(-x\): \(I = \displaystyle\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\dfrac{x^2\cos x\,e^x}{1 + e^x}\,dx\). Adding this to the original,

\(2I = \displaystyle\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}x^2\cos x\,dx = 2\int_0^{\pi/2}x^2\cos x\,dx\), so \(I = \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}x^2\cos x\,dx\).

By parts, \(\displaystyle\int x^2\cos x\,dx = x^2\sin x + 2x\cos x - 2\sin x\), so \(I = \dfrac{\pi^2}{4} - 2\).

So \(A = 4\), \(B = 2\) and \(\dfrac{A}{B} = 2\).

83.subtopic: Areas of Circles, Ellipses and Hyperbolas — Sectors, Segments and Standard Integrals
83.solution:
The smaller region lies between \(x = 1\) and \(x = 2\):

\(A = 2\displaystyle\int_1^2\sqrt{4 - x^2}\,dx = 2\left[\dfrac{x}{2}\sqrt{4 - x^2} + 2\sin^{-1}\dfrac{x}{2}\right]_1^2 = 2\left[\pi - \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\right] = \dfrac{4\pi}{3} - \sqrt{3}\).

84.subtopic: Area Under a Curve — Between a Curve and an Axis
84.solution:
In the first quadrant \(x = \sqrt{by}\). The area between the curve and the y-axis from \(y = 1\) to \(y = 4\) is

\(\displaystyle\int_1^4\sqrt{b}\,y^{1/2}\,dy = \sqrt{b} \cdot \dfrac{2}{3}\left[y^{3/2}\right]_1^4 = \sqrt{b} \cdot \dfrac{2}{3}(8 - 1) = \dfrac{14\sqrt{b}}{3}\).

\(\dfrac{14\sqrt{b}}{3} = 28\) gives \(\sqrt{b} = 6\), \(b = 36\).

85.solution:
\(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = e^{-y}(e^x + x^2)\), so \(e^y\,dy = (e^x + x^2)\,dx\).

Integrating: \(e^y = e^x + \dfrac{x^3}{3} + c\).

86.solution:
The determinant gives \(f f'' - (f')^2 = 0\), that is \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{f'}{f}\right) = \dfrac{f f'' - (f')^2}{f^2} = 0\).

So \(\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\) is constant, equal to \(\dfrac{f'(0)}{f(0)} = 2\). Hence \(f'(x) = 2f(x)\).

87.solution:
\(\dfrac{dy}{dx} - \dfrac{y}{x} = \dfrac{1}{x^2}\). The integrating factor is \(e^{-\int dx/x} = \dfrac{1}{x}\).

\(\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right) = \dfrac{1}{x^3}\), so \(\dfrac{y}{x} = -\dfrac{1}{2x^2} + c\).

Multiplying by \(2x^2\): \(2xy = -1 + 2cx^2\), that is \(2xy - 2cx^2 + 1 = 0\).

88.solution:
\(|\bar{a} + \bar{b}|^2 = 2 + 2\cos\theta = 4\cos^2\dfrac{\theta}{2}\) and \(|\bar{a} - \bar{b}|^2 = 2 - 2\cos\theta = 4\sin^2\dfrac{\theta}{2}\).

For \(0 < \theta < \pi\) both half-angle values are positive, so the ratio is \(\dfrac{2\cos(\theta/2)}{2\sin(\theta/2)} = \cot\dfrac{\theta}{2}\).

89.subtopic: Vector Geometry — Section Formula, Triangle, and Parallelogram
89.solution:
In a regular hexagon \(\overline{AB} = \overline{ED}\) and \(\overline{AF} = \overline{CD}\), so \(\overline{AB} + \overline{AE} = \overline{AE} + \overline{ED} = \overline{AD}\) and \(\overline{AC} + \overline{AF} = \overline{AC} + \overline{CD} = \overline{AD}\).

The sum is \(\overline{AD} + \overline{AD} + \overline{AD} = 3\overline{AD}\). As O is the midpoint of AD, \(\overline{AD} = 2\overline{AO}\), so the sum is \(6\overline{AO}\).

\(p = 3\), \(q = 6\).

91.solution:
\(\bar{a} + \bar{c} = -\bar{b}\), so \(|\bar{a} + \bar{c}|^2 = 25\): \(49 + 9 + 2\,\bar{a}\cdot\bar{c} = 25\), giving \(\bar{a}\cdot\bar{c} = -\dfrac{33}{2}\) and \(\cos(\bar{a} \wedge \bar{c}) = \dfrac{-33/2}{7 \times 3} = -\dfrac{11}{14}\).

With \(\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}\), \(-\dfrac{\pi}{4} = -\dfrac{22}{28} = -\dfrac{11}{14}\), so (B) holds.

Check the others: \(\bar{b} + \bar{c} = -\bar{a}\) gives \(25 + 9 + 2\,\bar{b}\cdot\bar{c} = 49\), \(\cos(\bar{b} \wedge \bar{c}) = \dfrac{15/2}{15} = \dfrac{1}{2}\), so \(\sin(\bar{b} \wedge \bar{c}) = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\): (A) and (C) fail. \(\sin(\bar{a} \wedge \bar{c}) = \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{121}{196}} = \dfrac{5\sqrt{3}}{14} \neq \dfrac{11}{14}\): (D) fails.

92.subtopic: Angles — Line, Plane, and Direction Conditions
92.solution:
Write both lines in standard form. First: \(\dfrac{x - 5}{5m + 2} = \dfrac{y - 2}{-5} = \dfrac{z - 1}{1}\), direction \((5m + 2, -5, 1)\).

Second: \(\dfrac{x}{1} = \dfrac{y + \frac{1}{2}}{2m} = \dfrac{z - 1}{3}\), direction \((1, 2m, 3)\).

Perpendicular: \((5m + 2) - 10m + 3 = 0\), so \(5 - 5m = 0\) and \(m = 1\).

93.subtopic: Line — Equation, Direction Cosines, and Vector Form
93.solution:
The line passes through \((-1, 2, -3)\) with direction \((1, 2, 3)\).

(A) \((-2, 0, -6)\) is on the line (each ratio is \(-1\)) and the direction is the same, so it is the same line.

(B) The plane's normal \((1, -2, 1)\) satisfies \((1, -2, 1)\cdot(1, 2, 3) = 0\), and \((-1, 2, -3)\) satisfies \(-1 - 4 - 3 + 8 = 0\), so the line lies in the plane.

(D) At \((0, 4, 0)\) each ratio is \(1\), so the line passes through it.

(C) For the line to be perpendicular to \(x - 2y + z = 0\), \((1, 2, 3)\) would have to be parallel to \((1, -2, 1)\); it is not. (C) is incorrect.

94.subtopic: Line — Equation, Direction Cosines, and Vector Form
94.solution:
A line perpendicular to both is along \((2, -3, 1) \times (1, 2, -2) = ((-3)(-2) - (1)(2),\ (1)(1) - (2)(-2),\ (2)(2) - (-3)(1)) = (4, 5, 7)\).

\(|(4, 5, 7)| = \sqrt{16 + 25 + 49} = \sqrt{90} = 3\sqrt{10}\).

The direction cosines are \(\pm\left(\dfrac{4}{3\sqrt{10}}, \dfrac{5}{3\sqrt{10}}, \dfrac{7}{3\sqrt{10}}\right)\), all three taking the same sign.

95.solution:
The lines pass through \((1, -1, 0)\) and \((-1, -1, 0)\). They are coplanar when \(\begin{vmatrix} -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & \lambda & 2 \\ 5 & 2 & \lambda \end{vmatrix} = -2(\lambda^2 - 4) = 0\), so \(\lambda = \pm 2\).

\(\lambda = 2\): normal \((2, 2, 2) \times (5, 2, 2) = (0, 6, -6)\), so the plane is \(y - z = c\); through \((1, -1, 0)\): \(y - z + 1 = 0\).

\(\lambda = -2\): normal \((2, -2, 2) \times (5, 2, -2) = (0, 14, 14)\), so the plane is \(y + z = c\); through \((1, -1, 0)\): \(y + z + 1 = 0\).

Together: \(y \pm z + 1 = 0\).

97.subtopic: Corner-Point Method — Maximum and Minimum of the Objective Function
97.solution:
The feasible region lies between the lines \(x + y = 1\) and \(2x + 3y = 6\) in the first quadrant. Its corners are \((1, 0)\), \((3, 0)\), \((0, 2)\) and \((0, 1)\).

\(Z\) there: \(3\), \(9\), \(2\), \(1\). The minimum is \(1\), at \((0, 1)\).

99.subtopic: Mean, Variance and Standard Deviation of a Binomial Variable
99.solution: The probabilities are \({}^3C_x\,p^x q^{3-x}\), so X is binomial with \(n = 3\). Its variance is \(npq = 3pq\).

100.subtopic: Conditional Probability, Independence and Bayes' Theorem
100.solution:
\(P(A \cap B) = P(A \mid B)P(B) = \dfrac{2}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{3}\).

\(P(A' \cup B) = 1 - P(A \cap B') = 1 - \left(\dfrac{2}{3} - \dfrac{1}{3}\right) = \dfrac{2}{3}\).

\(P(A \cup B') = 1 - P(A' \cap B) = 1 - \left(\dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{3}\right) = \dfrac{5}{6}\).

Sum \(= \dfrac{2}{3} + \dfrac{5}{6} = \dfrac{3}{2}\).

101.solution:
\(V = \pi r^2 L\), so \(\dfrac{\Delta V}{V} = 2\dfrac{\Delta r}{r} + \dfrac{\Delta L}{L}\).

The diameter \(4.0\) cm is measured to \(0.01\) cm, so \(\dfrac{\Delta r}{r} = \dfrac{\Delta d}{d} = \dfrac{0.01}{4.0} = 0.25\%\). The length gives \(\dfrac{0.1}{5.0} = 2\%\).

Percentage error \(= 2 \times 0.25\% + 2\% = 2.5\%\).

102.solution:
The sum of the two vectors is \(-\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}\).

\(\vec{A} + (-\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}) = \hat{j}\), so \(\vec{A} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k}\) and \(|\vec{A}| = \sqrt{1 + 4 + 1} = \sqrt{6}\).

103.solution: Both stones have the same acceleration g, so relative to each other they move uniformly. They start \(100\) m apart and close at \(25\) m/s, so they meet after \(\dfrac{100}{25} = 4\) s.

104.subtopic: Uniform Circular Motion — Centripetal Acceleration, Banking
104.solution:
Distance in x revolutions \(= x \cdot 2\pi r = x \cdot 2\pi \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{2} = \pi^2 x\).

\(v = \dfrac{\pi^2 x}{t}\).

105.solution:
Take \(m_1\)'s initial direction as positive. Before: \(m_1V_1 - m_2V_2\). After, the bodies have exchanged velocities: \(m_1\) moves back with \(V_2\) and \(m_2\) forward with \(V_1\), so the momentum is \(-m_1V_2 + m_2V_1\).

\(m_1V_1 - m_2V_2 = -m_1V_2 + m_2V_1\) gives \(m_1(V_1 + V_2) = m_2(V_1 + V_2)\), so \(\dfrac{m_2}{m_1} = 1\). (Velocities are exchanged in an elastic collision only between equal masses.)

106.solution: Power in rotation is \(P = \tau\omega\), and \(\tau = I\alpha\). So \(P = I\alpha\omega\) and \(\omega = \dfrac{P}{I\alpha}\).

107.solution:
No external torque acts, so the angular momentum \(L\) is conserved, and the rotational kinetic energy is \(\dfrac{L^2}{2I}\).

\(I = \dfrac{2}{5}MR^2\), so with \(R \to \dfrac{R}{3}\), \(I \to \dfrac{I}{9}\). Hence \(\dfrac{K_{\text{after}}}{K_{\text{before}}} = \dfrac{I}{I/9} = 9\).

108.subtopic: Variation of g with Depth, Altitude, Density, and Latitude
108.solution: At the equator \(g' = g - R\omega^2\). Setting \(g' = \dfrac{3}{5}g\): \(R\omega^2 = \dfrac{2}{5}g\), so \(\omega = \left(\dfrac{2g}{5R}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\).

109.solution:
Capillary rise \(h = \dfrac{2T\cos\theta}{r\rho g}\), so \(h \propto \dfrac{1}{r}\).

Area \(\pi r^2\) reduced to \(\dfrac{1}{3}\) means \(r \to \dfrac{r}{\sqrt{3}}\), so \(h \to \sqrt{3}h = 3\sqrt{3}\) cm.

110.solution:
Work to blow a bubble \(W = T \times 2 \times 4\pi r^2\) (two surfaces). Doubling the radius makes the area four times as large, so at the same surface tension the work would be four times.

Heating lowers the surface tension, so the work for the second bubble is slightly less than 4 times.

111.solution:
Excess pressure in a soap bubble \(= \dfrac{4T}{R}\), so \(P \propto \dfrac{1}{R}\). \(P_1 = 3P_2\) gives \(R_1 = \dfrac{R_2}{3}\).

\(\dfrac{V_1}{V_2} = \left(\dfrac{R_1}{R_2}\right)^3 = \dfrac{1}{27}\).

112.subtopic: Radiation — Stefan, Wien, Newton's Law of Cooling, Black Body
112.solution:
By Newton's law of cooling the excess over room temperature falls by the same factor in equal times.

In the first t minutes the excess falls from \(3\theta\) to \(2\theta\), a factor of \(\dfrac{2}{3}\). In the next t minutes it falls to \(2\theta \times \dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{4\theta}{3}\).

Temperature \(= \theta + \dfrac{4\theta}{3} = \dfrac{7\theta}{3}\). (The average-rate form of the law gives the same value.)

113.subtopic: Radiation — Stefan, Wien, Newton's Law of Cooling, Black Body
113.solution:
Power radiated \(= \sigma A T^4\) with \(A \propto R^2\). By Wien's law \(\lambda_m T = b\), so \(T \propto \dfrac{1}{\lambda}\).

So \(E \propto R^2\lambda^{-4}\).

114.subtopic: Radiation — Stefan, Wien, Newton's Law of Cooling, Black Body
114.solution: A black body emits all wavelengths, but not equally: its spectrum rises to a peak at \(\lambda_m\) (Wien's law) and falls on either side. So "power radiated is the same for all wavelengths" is wrong.

115.subtopic: Isothermal, Adiabatic, Isobaric, and Isochoric Processes
115.solution:
At constant pressure the volume and temperature both change. Work \(P\Delta V 
eq 0\), heat \(nC_p\Delta T 
eq 0\), and since the temperature changes, the internal energy changes too. So \(\Delta U 
eq 0\).

116.subtopic: Isothermal, Adiabatic, Isobaric, and Isochoric Processes
116.solution:
Sudden compression in an insulated container is adiabatic: \(PV^\gamma\) is constant, with \(\gamma = \dfrac{5}{3}\) for a monoatomic gas.

\(\dfrac{P_2}{P_1} = \left(\dfrac{V_1}{V_2}\right)^\gamma = 8^{5/3} = 2^5 = 32\).

117.subtopic: Kinetic Theory — Pressure, RMS Speed, and Temperature
117.solution: In a closed container the volume and amount of gas are fixed, so \(P \propto T\). The force on a wall is pressure times area, so it is proportional to \(T^1\).

118.subtopic: SHM Kinematics — Displacement, Velocity, Phase, and Damping
118.solution:
\(|v| = \omega\sqrt{A^2 - x^2} = \omega\sqrt{16 - 9} = \sqrt{7}\,\omega\) and \(|a| = \omega^2 x = 3\omega^2\).

Equal: \(3\omega^2 = \sqrt{7}\,\omega\), so \(\omega = \dfrac{\sqrt{7}}{3}\) and \(T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega} = \dfrac{6\pi}{\sqrt{7}}\) s.

119.subtopic: SHM Energy — Kinetic, Potential, and Total
119.solution:
From the mean position \(v = A\omega\cos\omega t\), so \(\dfrac{KE}{E} = \cos^2\omega t\).

\(\cos^2\omega t = \dfrac{1}{2}\) first at \(\omega t = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\), so \(t = \dfrac{T}{8} = \dfrac{6}{8} = 0.75\) s.

120.solution:
A small sphere sliding in a concave dish moves like a simple pendulum whose length is the radius of curvature.

\(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{R}{g}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{1.6}{10}} = 2\pi \times 0.4 = 0.8\pi\) s.

121.subtopic: Progressive Wave, Wave Equation, and Velocity
121.solution:
Wave speed on a string \(v = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}\), so \(T \propto v^2\). Three times the speed needs nine times the tension: \(9 \times 2 = 18\) kg wt.

Increase \(= 18 - 2 = 16\) kg wt.

122.subtopic: Pipes, Resonance Tube, and Doppler Effect
122.solution:
Fundamental of the closed pipe: \(f = \dfrac{v}{4L} = \dfrac{320}{4 \times 0.8} = 100\) Hz.

The string's first overtone is its second harmonic: \(f = \dfrac{2v_s}{2l} = \dfrac{v_s}{l}\), so \(v_s = 100 \times 0.5 = 50\) m/s.

\(v_s = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}\) gives \(\mu = \dfrac{50}{50^2} = 0.02\) kg/m, and the mass is \(0.02 \times 0.5 = 0.01\) kg \(= 10\) gram.

123.solution:
With p loops, \(f = \dfrac{p}{2l}\sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}\). The frequency and length are the same, so \(p\sqrt{T}\) is constant.

\(4\sqrt{1 \cdot g} = 2\sqrt{Mg}\), so \(\sqrt{M} = 2\) and \(M = 4\) kg.

124.solution: Every harmonic is proportional to \(\dfrac{1}{l}\) at fixed tension. With \(l \to 1.25l\), each frequency becomes \(\dfrac{1}{1.25} = 0.8\) of its value: the second harmonic decreases by \(20\%\) (from \(100\) Hz to \(80\) Hz).

125.solution: The number of lines of force is the flux \(\dfrac{q}{K\epsilon_0} = \dfrac{2 \times 8.85 \times 10^{-9}}{10 \times 8.85 \times 10^{-12}} = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{3}}{10} = 200\).

126.solution: Parallel: \(3C\). Series: \(\dfrac{C}{3}\). Equal energy: \(\dfrac{1}{2}(3C)V_p^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{C}{3}\right)V_s^2\), so \(\dfrac{V_p^2}{V_s^2} = \dfrac{1}{9}\) and \(V_p : V_s = 1 : 3\).

127.solution: A dielectric is polarised by the field between the plates, and its induced charges reduce the field. For the same charge the potential difference between the plates falls, so the capacitance \(C = \dfrac{Q}{V}\) rises. The dielectric reduces the effective potential on the plates.

128.solution:
\(C_4\) is connected directly across the battery, so \(Q_4 = 4C \cdot V = 4CV\).

\(C_3\), \(C_2\) and \(C_1\) form a series chain across the same two points: \(\dfrac{1}{C_s} = \dfrac{1}{3C} + \dfrac{1}{2C} + \dfrac{1}{C} = \dfrac{11}{6C}\), so \(C_s = \dfrac{6C}{11}\). Every capacitor in the chain carries the same charge, so \(Q_2 = \dfrac{6CV}{11}\).

\(\dfrac{Q_2}{Q_4} = \dfrac{6/11}{4} = \dfrac{3}{22}\).

130.solution:
\(S = \dfrac{G}{n - 1}\). The galvanometer and shunt share the current in inverse ratio of resistance:

\(\dfrac{I_g}{I} = \dfrac{S}{S + G} = \dfrac{G/(n-1)}{G/(n-1) + G} = \dfrac{1}{1 + (n - 1)} = \dfrac{1}{n}\).

131.subtopic: Classification, Curie's Law, Hysteresis, and Shielding
131.solution: Curie's law, \(\chi = \dfrac{C}{T}\), holds for paramagnetic substances, so \(\chi T\) is constant for them. Diamagnetic susceptibility hardly depends on temperature, and ferromagnets follow a different law (Curie-Weiss above the Curie point).

132.chapter: Magnetic Fields Due to Electric Current
132.subtopic: Magnetic Moment of Current Loop and Galvanometer Instruments
132.solution:
The wire length is fixed: \(N\pi d = N'\pi(2d)\), so \(N' = \dfrac{N}{2}\).

\(m = NIA\) with \(A \propto d^2\): \(\dfrac{m'}{m} = \dfrac{N/2}{N} \times 4 = 2\). The ratio is \(2 : 1\).

133.chapter: Magnetic Fields Due to Electric Current
133.subtopic: Force on Moving Charge in Magnetic Field
133.solution: The magnetic force \(q(\vec{V} \times \vec{B})\) is always perpendicular to the velocity, so its power \(\vec{F}\cdot\vec{V}\) is zero at every instant. It changes the direction of motion but does no work.

134.subtopic: Faraday's and Lenz's Laws — Induced EMF, Current, and Charge
134.solution:
Induced emf \(e = \dfrac{n(\Phi_1 - \Phi_2)}{t}\) (the options write the time as T). Total resistance \(= R + \dfrac{R}{4} = \dfrac{5R}{4}\).

\(I = \dfrac{e}{5R/4} = \dfrac{4n(\Phi_1 - \Phi_2)}{5Rt}\).

135.solution: \(e = M\dfrac{\Delta I}{\Delta t}\), so \(\Delta t = \dfrac{M\,\Delta I}{e} = \dfrac{3 \times 5}{4000} = 3.75 \times 10^{-3}\) s.

136.subtopic: Faraday's and Lenz's Laws — Induced EMF, Current, and Charge
136.solution: Inside the pipe the falling magnet induces eddy currents that oppose its motion (Lenz's law), so it falls with acceleration less than g. Once it has left the pipe there is no conductor around it, no eddy current and no opposing force, so it falls freely with \(9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}\).

137.subtopic: Power in AC Circuit — Average, Factor, Wattless

138.subtopic: Reactance — Inductive, Capacitive, and Single-Element Circuits
138.solution: \(X_C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi fC}\), so \(f = \dfrac{1}{2\pi C X_C} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi \times 10^{-5} \times 2 \times 10^{-3}} = \dfrac{10^{8}}{4\pi}\) Hz \(= \dfrac{25}{\pi}\) MHz.

139.subtopic: Reactance — Inductive, Capacitive, and Single-Element Circuits
139.solution: (The \(3\) H is the coil's inductance.) Inductive reactance is \(X_L = 2\pi fL\). On a.c. it is finite and non-zero; on d.c. \(f = 0\), so \(X_L = 0\). The ratio a.c. to d.c. is therefore infinite.

140.subtopic: Lenses — Lens Formula, Power, and Lensmaker
140.solution:
Cutting along the vertical axis splits the lens through its thickness into two plano-convex lenses. For the equiconvex lens \(\dfrac{1}{F} = (\mu - 1)\dfrac{2}{R}\); each half has one curved face and one flat face, so \(\dfrac{1}{f} = (\mu - 1)\dfrac{1}{R} = \dfrac{1}{2F}\).

Each part has focal length \(2F\).

141.subtopic: Refraction, Apparent Depth, and Total Internal Reflection

142.subtopic: Single Slit Diffraction and Resolving Power
142.solution: The angular positions of the minima are set by \(a\sin\theta = n\lambda\), which depends only on \(\lambda\) and the slit width \(a\). Moving the screen changes the linear spacing on it but not the angular separation, which remains the same.

143.subtopic: Single Slit Diffraction and Resolving Power
143.solution: Width of the central maximum \(= \dfrac{2\lambda D}{a}\). Setting it equal to \(a\): \(\dfrac{2\lambda D}{a} = a\), so \(D = \dfrac{a^2}{2\lambda}\).

144.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
144.subtopic: Photoelectric Effect — Stopping Potential, Threshold, and Work Function
144.solution: \(eV_0 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} - \phi\). A shorter wavelength means more energetic photons, so the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons, and with it the stopping potential, increases.

145.solution: Bohr's condition \(2\pi r_n = n\lambda_n\) with \(r_n \propto n^2\) gives \(\lambda_n \propto n\). The third excited state is \(n = 4\), so the de Broglie wavelength becomes four times as large: it increases.

146.solution: In the nth orbit \(E \propto \dfrac{1}{n^2}\) and \(L = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi} \propto n\). Hence \(E \propto L^{-2}\).

148.solution: A photodiode is operated in reverse bias. Light falling on the junction creates electron-hole pairs, and the reverse current grows with the intensity of the light while hardly depending on the bias voltage. So (D) is correct and (A), (B) and (C) are not.

149.subtopic: p-n Junction — Depletion Layer and Biasing
149.solution: Under reverse bias only a tiny current flows until the reverse voltage is raised to the breakdown value, when the current rises sharply (Zener or avalanche breakdown). Breakdown is reached by increasing the reverse bias.

150.subtopic: p-n Junction — Depletion Layer and Biasing
150.solution: Forward bias opposes the barrier potential, so the barrier voltage falls and the depletion layer narrows. Majority carriers cross the junction and the diode conducts.
